metadata.title: Parents’ Impact on Students’ Reading Achievement
metadata.venue: Proceedings of the International Scientific Conference. Volume III, May 22th -23th, 2020. 656-666

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 microdata (students’ tests plus students’ and parents’ questionnaires) and conducts country-level linear regression analyses. The manuscript does not report whether PIRLS complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) were applied, nor does it name any weight variables or replicate-weight procedures. Because the analysis is described as linear regression and correlation/frequency analysis at the country level, the paper provides no explicit guidance on weight usage for population-representative inference. Analysts using PIRLS IDB should apply the official PIRLS sampling weights and replicate weights when estimating standard errors, but this paper’s weighting strategy is not documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper models PIRLS reading literacy achievement as the dependent variable but does not describe how missing questionnaire/test responses were handled (e.g., complete-case exclusion vs. imputation). This is a reporting gap because PIRLS datasets typically contain item nonresponse, and the choice of missing-data handling can affect regression coefficients and statistical significance. The manuscript also does not document plausible-value usage for the achievement outcome, so PV handling cannot be verified from the text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper analyzes PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading literacy achievement and links it to parents’ preschool-age reading-promotion activities. The dependent variable is students’ reading literacy achievement in Grade 4, and the key independent variables are parents’ reported activity frequencies (often vs. never/almost never) plus a parental activity index (average across activities). The study includes additional controls for parents’ education (converted to years of schooling), students’ gender, the use of the test language at home, and preschool attendance duration (3 or more than 3 years). The manuscript does not report any further inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., complete-case only, missing response handling, or specific country subsamples) beyond the stated focus on parents’ responses and the country-level research unit.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (linear regression coefficients by country; statistical significance at 95% indicated by asterisks in Table 3).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading the study leveraged Parental activity index (average), Parents’ education (years), Test language at home, Preschool attended 3+ years, and Child’s gender to predict Reading literacy achievement (PIRLS RA), finding that the parental activity index was statistically significant in all countries except Georgia and South Africa. This indicates that strengthening parents’ preschool reading-promotion activities is associated with higher Grade 4 reading literacy, though the paper does not establish causal effects and does not report PV/missing-data handling.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (country-level regression by activity)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (nine activity-specific regression coefficients by country; Table 2 reports coefficient ranges MIN=-19 to MAX=99 and marks statistically significant coefficients at 95%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading the study leveraged Read books often, Tell stories often, Sing songs often, Alphabet toys often, and Write letters/words often to predict Reading literacy achievement (PIRLS RA), finding that reading together (read books) showed the most consistently positive associations across countries, storytelling was also effective, while some activities (e.g., alphabet toys, singing songs, and talking about things done) showed minimal impact and writing letters/words had a negative statistically significant association in Latvia. This indicates that early parent-child shared reading and storytelling may be prioritized in preschool literacy programs, while some fine-grained activities may require timing/quality guidance rather than being assumed universally beneficial.

data.outcome_summary: The paper analyzes PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading literacy achievement using parents’ preschool-age activity reports and related student/family questionnaire variables, with a country as the research unit. It reports linear regression results (plus frequency/correlation analysis) showing that parents’ education is a statistically considerable factor for reading achievement in most participant countries (except Hong Kong) and that the parental activity index (average across multiple activities) is statistically significant in all countries except Georgia and South Africa. The activity-specific regressions suggest the strongest positive associations for reading books together and storytelling, while several other activities show minimal effects; notably, writing letters/words is negatively associated with reading achievement in Latvia. The study does not report survey-weight usage, plausible-value handling, or missing-data strategy, and it does not provide ML model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC), limiting interpretability and causal claims.
